name: The Drowning Count
description: Held on the last Sunday of August each year, the Drowning Count marks the anniversary of the 2201 Lake Michigan Surge Event, when a combination of catastrophic infrastructure failure and a corponation-suppressed weather system warning caused the flooding of eleven the Gray Zone districts, killing an estimated 23,000 residents over four days. The name comes from the Gray Zone practice of reading names aloud — 'the Count' — for as many hours as communities can sustain, with different neighborhoods taking relay shifts so the names never stop from sundown Saturday to sundown Sunday. The official corponation response was a memorial holo-sculpture installed in Tier 3's Lakefront Promenade, which most the Gray Zone residents have never seen.
cultural_impact: The Drowning Count has become the emotional center of the Gray Zone civic identity — the one day when even rival neighborhood factions set aside territorial disputes, when synthetic residents are explicitly welcomed as equal mourners, and when Tier 2 workers who lost family in the surge quietly cross the tier boundary to stand with the Gray Zone communities. It is also the single day most feared by corporate PR departments, as investigative leaks reliably surface around it each year.
locations: The Silt Wall, South the Gray Zone waterfront
Drowned District marker, former the Gray Zone Ward 7
story_hooks: Sediment, the E.L.F. archivist who has maintained the complete name registry for twenty years, detects that 847 names were quietly removed from the official count after the first year — names belonging to unregistered synthetic workers who were in the flooded districts. Recovering and restoring those names before sundown Sunday becomes a desperate race against corporate data-scrubbing.

A Tier 4 Nakamura-Voss infrastructure engineer attends the Drowning Count in secret, knowing that their division holds suppressed engineering reports proving the surge was preventable — and that sitting in the relay count for hours might finally break their silence.

A young the Gray Zone artist has created an unauthorized augmented-reality overlay that, when viewed through any BCI near the Lakefront Promenade's official memorial sculpture, replaces it with the faces of the uncounted dead — and the corponation wants it shut down before it goes viral on Founder's Debt Day.
origin_event: The Lake Michigan Surge Event of August 2201, in which suppressed flood-warning data and deliberate infrastructure underfunding caused the inundation of eleven the Gray Zone wards. The first Drowning Count was organized by survivor Perpetua Dąbrowski-Okafor in 2202 using handwritten name lists compiled from neighborhood memory, as official casualty records were sealed under corporate liability protection orders.
tier_observations: Tier 1 residents organize the relay reading in shifts, with entire families holding spots through the night, bringing food to share and candles made from salvaged wax. Tier 2 workers with surge connections attend quietly, often not speaking, standing at the edges of the relay circles. Tier 3 residents largely observe through curated memorial content on corporate media feeds, rarely attending in person. Tier 4 and 5 are almost entirely absent; some Tier 4 employees make private charitable donations to the Gray Zone flood-resilience funds as a guilt-offset. The official Tier 3-4 corporate memorial at Lakefront Promenade holds a brief sponsored sunrise ceremony attended primarily by PR staff.
